But if everyone used that zero to four kilohertz band on the same line, well, then all the conversations would be on top of each other and you wouldn't be able to hear the person that you're talking to.
Luckily, we can shift those electrical signals, so my conversation can use zero to four kilohertz while another person's can use four to eight and so on all the way down the same copper wire.
At the other end, a filter separates out the different frequency bands, similar to how a radio can tune into one station.
Then the signal is shifted back down to the zero to four kilohertz range before it hits the speaker, so it sounds like a normal voice.
But as phone companies started using higher and higher frequencies, they started running into problems.
That oscillating current carrying the signal generates additional fields, a magnetic field shown here in red, and little loops of current called eddy currents, which are shown here in blue.

Now, because of their shape, those loops resist changes to the current at the center of the wire, and they reinforce changes along the surface, but eddy currents get stronger the faster the signal changes.
And if you want more calls, you need more bands, which use higher and higher frequencies.

But if the signal can only travel along the wire's surface, it's limited to a smaller cross section.

For a while, telephone companies were able to work around the high loss by boosting signals every few kilometers.
But past 65 megahertz, well, the high frequencies died off in less than two kilometers, so they were too impractical to use.
And this trade-off between signal power and data rate was actually discovered back in 1948.
The Shannon-Hartley theorem described the maximum capacity of a communication channel based on the signal power, noise, and bandwidth, or the difference between the highest and lowest frequencies.
The best way to increase capacity is to increase the bandwidth.

When the wave meets a boundary at an angle, one end of the crest crosses into the new material first, and it changes speed before the rest.
If light travels slower in that new material, then that end drags behind and the beam bends or refracts away from the boundary.
How much it bends depends on the angle it hits the boundary and on how much each material slows light down, which is described by their index of refraction.
This relationship is defined by Snell's Law.

So Kao knew that if the high loss wasn't from light leaking out the sides, well, it had to be from something else.
He spoke with material scientists and glass experts, but no one seemed to know what was really causing it.
He kept looking and eventually he landed on two potential sources: scattering and absorption.

If you shine light through a perfect crystal that's transparent, there's going to be a little bit of reflection, but almost all of the electromagnetic energy will keep going down in the same direction that it started.
But glass isn't a crystalline solid.
The basic building block is silica or silicon dioxide, one silicon atom connected to four oxygen atoms in a tetrahedra or pyramid shape.
In the glass, the pyramids are connected at the corners, so every oxygen is shared with another silicon.
That's why it's called silicon dioxide.
For every two oxygens, there's one silicon atom.
This is an amorphous solid.
Unlike a crystal, its atoms have no long-range order.
Instead, its disordered liquid-like structure locks in as it cools, with the exact arrangement depending on the glass type and cooling speed.
For example, if you quench the glass really fast, the structure locks at a higher temperature.
The final solid has lots of dense regions, which re-radiate more light than the sparse ones.
The light scatters, which weakens the signal.
This is called Rayleigh scattering, and you can't get rid of it completely, but if you cool the glass slowly, those pyramids have more time to settle and pack together evenly.
The structure locks in at a lower temperature and light scatters less.
But Kao needed to know the minimum scattering.
Was it 10 decibels a kilometer, a hundred, a thousand?
He needed something concrete.

Kao used his calculations to estimate that if the glass's structure was locked at a thousand degrees Celsius, well, its scattering loss would be around one decibel a kilometer.
He was surprised.

That's what causes more density fluctuations, but a thousand degrees Celsius was pretty hot compared to other glass types, so then scattering couldn't be behind those crazy high losses.
Absorption had to be the problem, but Kao didn't know what exactly was absorbing so much light.

Well, absorption works like this.

In a single atom, electrons sit at discrete energy levels, and there are usually some empty spaces in the upper ones, but pack atoms together into a solid and those levels smear up into wide bands separated by gaps.
Now when light hits the surface, it can excite an electron to a higher band, but only if the photon has at least as much energy as this band gap.
If it does, the photon is absorbed and eventually it releases that energy as heat.
In something like silicon, that band gap is very small.

It's got plenty of energy, so it gets absorbed.

Visible light doesn't have enough energy, so it passes right through, and that's why glass looked clear to us.
